<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early mortality after long-term care facility (LTCF) admission is common; yet, prognostic tools are often derived from Western minimum dataset-based cohorts or require hospital electronic health record linkages that are unavailable at intake in many LTCFs. There is also limited evidence on explainable, admission-feasible machine learning–based prognostication in Asian LTCF settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aim of the study is to develop and temporally externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting 6-month all-cause mortality among older adults newly admitted to LTCFs in Taiwan using routinely collected LTCF assessment data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the JUBO Long-Term Care Database, a nationwide private administrative registry covering 636 LTCFs (37.4% of the national LTCFs) in Taiwan. We included residents with first-time LTCF admission and prespecified nonoverlapping cohorts for temporal validation: development (January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2023; n=23,901) and external validation (January 1 to December 31, 2024; n=6216). The outcome measure was death within 180 days of admission. We compared a nonlinear ensemble model (hybrid of extreme gradient boosting and random forest [HybridXGBRF]) with 7 other algorithms, including tree-based and linear benchmarks. Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC]), classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, and
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      ), and calibration (Brier score and calibration plots) were assessed. Model interpretability was examined using Shapley Additive Explanations.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the development cohort, 5272 of 23,901 (22.1%) residents died within 180 days. In the 2024 temporal validation cohort, 1781 of 6216 (28.7%) residents died. In internal cross-validation, HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models (0.89, 95% CI 0.88‐0.89). In temporal validation, HybridXGBRF maintained strong discrimination (AUROC 0.90, 95% CI 0.89‐0.91), with an accuracy of 0.85 and an
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.68. Calibration plots indicated close agreement between predicted and observed risks across most probability ranges, with mild divergences at higher predicted risks. Shapley Additive Explanations analysis identified frequent hospitalizations within 6 months, activities of daily living impairment, and weight loss as influential predictors. The model showed stable AUROC across sex and age strata (0.89‐0.90) and maintained high discrimination among residents with improving activities of daily living scores (AUROC 0.91, 95% CI 0.90‐0.92).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An interpretable machine learning model using routinely collected Taiwanese LTCF assessment data achieved strong discrimination, acceptable calibration, and stable temporal validation performance without requiring hospital-based electronic health record linkage. The HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models, but performance differences from extreme gradient boosting were small. The model may serve as a risk-stratification tool to help identify residents who could benefit from structured care review, advance care planning, or palliative care assessment. Prospective implementation studies could determine its impact on care processes and resident- or family-centered outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development and Temporal External Validation of a Parsimonious, Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Predicting 6-Month Mortality in Long-Term Care Facilities: A Retrospective Cohort Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This exploratory study examines changes in depressive symptoms following spousal loss relative to remaining married across countries, whether these associations vary by national context and gender, and the extent to which selection into widowhood accounts for cross-national differences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study uses data from the Health and Retirement Study international family of studies and evaluates change in depressive symptoms across six country contexts: United States, England, Mexico, China, and two combinations of European Union countries categorized by welfare state: Conservative and Social/Democratic. We evaluated change in depressive symptoms among individuals who were married at Wave 1 (2015/2016 depending on country) and at Wave 2 (2018) when some remained married while others reported a spousal loss. The analytic sample included adults aged 60 years and older (Wave 1 mean age = 69.13 years, standard deviation [SD] = 6.78).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using ordinary least squares regression and propensity score methods to account for selection into widowhood, results suggest that the experience of widowhood is generally similar across country contexts, with widows experiencing, on average, about 0.5 SDs increase in depressive symptoms (marginal effect = 0.53, p &lt; .001; propensity adjusted score = 0.56, p &lt; .001), a likely clinically relevant increase, accounting for selection. These effects were roughly the same for men and women in all country contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future research is needed to identify factors that may buffer the consequences of widowhood and explore university and cross-national interventions that may help reduce these effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Changes in Depressive Symptoms Associated with Spousal Loss in Six Country Contexts

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults often face significant barriers to mental health help-seeking. This study integrated participatory co-design with behavioural science principles to develop culturally meaningful hybrid nudges to normalise mental health help-seeking among older adults in Hong Kong.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twelve older adults with mental health volunteering experience participated in eight researcher-facilitated co-design workshops structured by design thinking principles. A graphic designer assisted in visualising the prototypes. Workshop artefacts, design outputs, structured summaries, and focus group recordings were analysed using thematic analysis. The study was primarily an intervention development study; focus group data were used as an embedded process evaluation to understand participants’ experiences of co-design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Co-designers were 75% female with a mean age of 63.83 years. The co-design process produced a set of hybrid nudge prototypes with two design orientations: (1) reminiscence-oriented using metaphors from childhood games to cue autonomy and peer support, and (2) psychoeducation-oriented using relatable vignettes to model perspective taking. Although the project initially aimed to create social norms and visual nudges, co-designers preferred integrating brief psychoeducational and general well-being content to increase acceptability. The embedded process evaluation highlighted perceived learning, ownership, and collaboration, as well as challenges such as self-doubt.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participatory co-design can support the development of theory-informed and culturally attuned hybrid nudges to address motivational barriers to mental health help-seeking. Future research should test acceptability and behavioural outcomes through randomized or pragmatic trials, and examine how to balance theoretical fidelity with participant agency in co-designed behavioural interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Developing hybrid nudges to promote mental health help-seeking in Chinese older adults: A co-design approach

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping many aspects of dementia care, and end-of-life caregiving for persons with dementia may not be exempt from such paradigm shifts. In this study, we explored families’ and staff’s acceptance of AI in hospice dementia care and generated actionable recommendations for AI designers in supporting end-of-life care for persons with dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted individual and focus group interviews with family caregivers (N = 30) of hospice patients with dementia and hospice staff (N = 9). We utilized the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as our theoretical framework and conducted directed content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants described AI tools as potentially helpful for obtaining information, monitoring patients, managing medications and appointments, providing companionship, and conducting logistical tasks. Familiarity with technology, along with user-friendly interfaces and guidance, emerged as subcategories of perceived ease of use. The uniqueness of hospice, encompassing its humanistic nature and emphasis on families as part of the care unit, also emerged as a key factor impacting attitudes towards AI use. Although many anticipated that AI would bring inevitable changes in the future, they showed nuanced trust and perspectives on how it would impact the essence of care. Based on our participants’ narratives, recommendations emerged across three domains: population-related, AI feature-related, and deployment-related.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Families and frontline staff should not be considered merely as end users, but as key stakeholders whose needs and expertise should shape the direction of AI applications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Is there a role for artificial intelligence in end-of-life care for persons with dementia? Perspectives of and recommendations by caregivers and hospice staff

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prevalence of vision impairment continues to increase globally due to population growth and aging. Among older adults with vision impairment, loneliness is common. Prior studies assessing loneliness risk have relied on regression-based approaches, which may not capture complex, heterogeneous conditional pathways. We apply a theoretically guided machine learning approach to examine loneliness risk among older adults with age-related macular degeneration (AMD).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using baseline data from 210 adults with AMD (Agemean = 80.1 years) enrolled in a randomized controlled trial, we applied a decision tree method using measures of legal blindness, emotional responses to vision loss, social life satisfaction, anxiety, depression, optimism, future planning, and sociodemographic factors to investigate heterogeneous pathways to loneliness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Decision tree models demonstrated stable discrimination (AUCtrain=.88, AUCtest=.78, DeLong 95% CI: 0.68–0.88) and robust classification performance across thresholds. Social life satisfaction emerged as the primary branching condition differentiating loneliness outcomes. Distinct pathways suggested that high social life satisfaction was strongly associated with lower loneliness; optimism served as a compensatory resource when social satisfaction was lower. Additional pathways highlighted the effects of vision loss severity, anxiety, and emotional responses to vision loss on loneliness. Depressive symptoms differentiated loneliness outcomes within a lower-anxiety branch, suggesting depression may overshadow protective factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that loneliness arises through heterogeneous psychological pathways rather than single risk factors. By identifying conditional configurations of psychosocial and health-related factors, interpretable decision-tree models may inform more targeted screening, evaluation, and intervention strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Conditional pathways to loneliness in older adults with vision impairment: A decision-tree analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atypical survey response patterns, such as inconsistent or implausible responses, have been linked to lower cognitive functioning in later life. This study examined whether these behaviors predict future dementia onset across diverse longitudinal studies of aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a coordinated analysis of data from eight longitudinal studies of aging (total N = 76,350). We derived five common types of atypical response pattern indicators from participants’ questionnaire data. Associations with subsequent dementia risk were examined within each cohort using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic covariates and accounting for death as a competing risk. Results were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis methods.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across cohorts, significant associations with incident dementia were observed for item-nonresponse (overall hazard ratio [HR] per SD increase = 1.06), random response errors (HR = 1.25), multivariate outlier responses (HR = 1.31), and incompatible response patterns indexed by Guttman errors and person-fit statistics (HRs = 1.22–1.25). Extreme responding was not significantly associated with dementia risk. Secondary analyses suggested stronger associations among individuals younger than 75 years and those with higher levels of education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Routine survey responses contain behavioral signals associated with emerging dementia risk. Because these indicators can be derived from existing survey data without additional testing burden, they may provide a scalable complement to traditional approaches for studying cognitive aging in large population-based cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Atypical survey response patterns as early indicators of dementia onset: A coordinated analysis across longitudinal aging cohorts

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sociological theory posits that social networks function as enduring relational structures that constrain and enable everyday social interactions, yet empirical evidence linking network properties to real-time social exposures remains limited. To address this gap, this study examines how older adults' social networks are associated with their daily social experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas (SECHURA) study, we combine egocentric network data (1,474 alters from 254 respondents) with ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data capturing real-time social interactions over one week (5,342 observations). We evaluate associations between three network properties–structure (quantity, composition, and interconnectedness of network members), heterogeneity (diversity in gender, race/ethnicity, and age), and strength (strong and supportive ties) – and four momentary outcomes (number and type of interaction partners, social activities, and being outside the home).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Random-effects models show that larger and more socially diverse networks are associated with greater momentary social engagement, including more interaction partners, less time alone, and more explicit socializing. Both role diversity and network density are associated with heightened social exposure, through distinct pathways. Sociodemographic heterogeneity also predicts interaction patterns, with age heterogeneity linked to kin-centered interactions and racial heterogeneity to non-kin exposure. Stronger affective ties predicted less engagement in explicit socializing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Personal social networks operate as critical structures linked to the quantity, composition, and context of older adults' real-time social exposures. Large, densely connected, and role-diverse networks appear to facilitate everyday interactions through different mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations between social network characteristics and daily social experiences in later life: Evidence from ecological momentary assessment

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subjective cognitive impairment (SCI) predicts Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Identifying SCI correlates may identify cognitive risk earlier in the ADRD continuum. We examined SCI correlates among older non-Hispanic Black (NHB) and non-Hispanic White (NHW) men.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cross-sectional data were from 669 men in the 2012 National Health and Aging Trends Study. Logistic regression was used to identify SCI correlates, accounting for complex sampling and attrition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Result</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher education (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.13–0.87) and former smoking (OR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.16–0.91) were associated with lower SCI odds. Sleep difficulties (OR = 2.81, 95% CI: 1.22–6.47), multimorbidity (OR = 2.16, 95% CI: 1.09–4.29), and ADL disability (OR = 4.19, 95% CI: 2.03–8.61) were associated with higher odds.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Education, smoking status, sleep, multimorbidity, and functional status may be important SCI correlates among older NHB and NHW men. Addressing modifiable correlates may support cognitive health earlier in the ADRD continuum.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines associations between neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage during adolescence and early adulthood and chronic disease accumulation in mid- to late life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using Panel Study of Income Dynamics data linked to U.S. Census and American Community Survey data, we identify four trajectories of neighborhood disadvantage, namely persistent disadvantage, increasing disadvantage, decreasing disadvantage, and persistent advantage, and estimate their associations with chronic and cardiometabolic conditions diagnosed between ages 40 and 75.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with persistent neighborhood advantage, persistent and increasing disadvantage are associated with chronic disease burden, net of individual and contemporaneous neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. Associations between decreasing disadvantage and multimorbidity are largely attenuated after adjustment for individual socioeconomic characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Persistent neighborhood disadvantage is associated with greater chronic disease accumulation, while worsening disadvantage is particularly associated with cardiometabolic burden, highlighting the relevance of earlier-life inequality for aging. Adolescence and early adulthood may represent sensitive periods, with early adulthood potentially more consequential for chronic disease burden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Life Course Neighborhood Socioeconomic Disadvantage and Chronic Disease Accumulation in Mid- to Late Adulthood

records.abstract: <jats:p>A sense of purpose is a central component of mental well-being in older adulthood. Although many predictors of purpose have been identified, most studies have considered a limited set, leaving their relative importance unclear. The present study addressed this gap by examining a large set of psychological, social, and demographic variables in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults from the Health and Retirement Study. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) was used to evaluate 47 predictors. Self-esteem emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by positive affect. The leading predictors were organized into six domains: adaptive self-related beliefs, affective well-being, perceived control, optimism, social engagement, and spirituality/religiosity. Demographic variables were less predictive overall. These findings indicate that individual differences in purpose are associated with a broad set of psychological resources involving self-regulation, interpersonal processes, optimism, and positive affect.</jats:p>
title: Purpose in Life Among Older Adults: A Machine Learning Analysis of Potential Predictors

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 2024 U.S. federal minimum staffing rule for nursing homes was vacated and repealed before taking effect, but states continue to adopt their own standards. Whether uniform standards impose uneven compliance burdens is unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine whether the 2024 federal minimums differed by neighborhood deprivation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cross-sectional analysis of 9,315 U.S. nursing homes linking CMS-reported staffing (April to June 2025) with the Area Deprivation Index (ADI).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, 42.8%, 67.0%, and 31.3% of facilities staffed below the registered nurse (RN), nurse aide, and total nursing minimums, respectively. Facilities in the most deprived tercile staffed 0.103 RN hours per resident day lower than the least deprived (95% CI, −0.161 to −0.045), with 2.28 times the odds of falling below the RN minimum.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Uniform staffing standards would concentrate compliance burden on facilities serving deprived urban communities. Future state or federal standards should pair minimums with financing and workforce supports.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Neighborhood Deprivation and Nursing Home Staffing Gaps Relative to the 2024 U.S. Federal Minimum Staffing Standards

                    <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) reflects older adults’ physical and mental abilities, and its decline predicts loss of independence. <jats:p>
                    Elder clowning is a multi-component, person-centred intervention delivered to persons living with dementia in long-term care to enhance quality of life through individualised social engagement. Although persons with dementia are the target recipients of the intervention, their families may also derive benefits. However, their perspectives currently remain unexplored. This study aimed to explore whether and in what ways families of persons living with dementia in long-term care benefit from elder clowning interventions, from the perspectives of families and long-term care staff. Semi-structured interviews with family members of persons living with dementia and long-term care staff were conducted in four long-term care homes in Eastern Australia. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed according to Braun and Clarke’s Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Analysis of family member (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 11) and staff (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 20) perspectives on elder clowning generated two main themes: (1) transforming the emotional experience of visiting and (2) strengthening family connections through the shared experience. Elder clowning supported families to have improved visiting experiences with their relative in long-term care, which eased visit-related stress before, during, and after visits. Person-centred engagement through elder clowning was perceived to support the reciprocal interaction and happiness of their relative, which supported positive emotions for families. Families learned about their relative’s communicative capacity and new dementia-specific communication skills, which they then implemented independently from elder clowning. Shared positive experiences supported socialisation, reminiscence, and memory-making, which may have supported family connections. Elder clowning also provided families with opportunities for social support. While some families were actively involved, others preferred to watch, and some were perceived to decline involvement. Families expressed preferences or suggestions regarding intervention delivery, such as continuity and access. The benefits of elder clowning were found to extend beyond entertainment to support psychosocial wellbeing of families of persons living with dementia in long-term care.
                  </jats:p>
title: “Someone’s Acknowledged My Mum…in that Moment she Connected”: A Qualitative Study of Family Benefits of Elder Clowning for Persons With Dementia in Long-Term Care

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse (CCW) algorithms are widely used to identify chronic conditions in Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) claims. However, their validity in Medicare Advantage (MA) encounters remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a cross-sectional study using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare data. We analyzed NHATS Rounds 9 and 11, aged≥65 years, with continuous 24-month enrollment in MA or FFS. CCW algorithms were applied to identify six conditions: arthritis, chronic lung disease, diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, and osteoporosis. Self-reported, physician-diagnosed conditions from NHATS interviews served as the reference standard. Survey-weighted sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and balanced accuracy were compared between MA and FFS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We included 1,708 MA and 2,239 FFS beneficiaries in Round 9 and 1,472 MA and 1,566 FFS beneficiaries in Round 11. Across both rounds, balanced accuracy was similar between MA and FFS for all six conditions. Diabetes and hypertension demonstrated high sensitivity (0.88–0.94), while arthritis and osteoporosis showed lower sensitivity but high specificity. Although statistically significant MA–FFS differences were observed for select metrics (diabetes PPV in Round 9; chronic lung disease specificity in Round 11), absolute differences were minor and not clinically meaningful.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CCW algorithms perform comparably in MA and FFS Medicare data. These findings support the validity of using CCW algorithms in MA encounter data for epidemiologic research for risk adjustment, facilitating more generalizable studies of the growing MA population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Performance of Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-For-Service Populations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evidence comparing the performance of claims-based dementia algorithms across Medicare Advantage (MA) and fee-for-service (FFS) populations remains limited. We evaluated the validity of two claims-based algorithms across MA and FFS populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used nationally representative, linked National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS)-Medicare data to identify community-dwelling participants with continuous enrollment in MA or FFS during Round 7 (2017; n = 5,018), Round 9 (2019; n = 4,018), and Round 11 (2021-2022; n = 3,086). Using NHATS probable dementia as reference standard, we validated the Bynum-Standard and Chronic Condition Warehouse (CCW) dementia algorithms across three time points.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, both algorithms demonstrated comparable performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity (&gt;97.9%) and negative predictive value [NPV] (&gt;92.9%). The Bynum algorithm showed similar sensitivity between MA and FFS in Rounds 7 (30.2% vs. 29.1%) and 11 (25.6% vs. 23.9%), but lower sensitivity in MA for Round 9 (25.0% vs. 36.4%). Positive predictive value [PPV] was similar between MA (62.7%-70.6%) and FFS (62.1%-70.4%) across all rounds. The CCW algorithm demonstrated greater MA-FFS differences, with lower sensitivity in MA for Rounds 9 (30.8% vs. 46.9%) and 11 (35.0% vs. 49.3%) and similar sensitivity for Round 7 (40.4% vs. 42.2%). PPV varied across rounds in both MA and FFS [(Round 7: 76.3% vs. 71.2%) to (Round 11: 68.5% vs. 76.4%)]. Both algorithms identified participants with more severe dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Claims-based dementia algorithms demonstrate broadly consistent performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity and moderate PPV but comparable or lower sensitivity in MA, informing case ascertainment across Medicare plan type.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Performance of Claims-based Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite growing enrollment in Medicare Advantage (MA) plans, the performance of claims-based frailty algorithms, which were developed for Medicare fee-for-service (FFS), remains unclear in MA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We calculated the Kim claims-based frailty index (CFI), Veterans Affairs-Frailty Index (VA-FI), and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS) using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) and MA data. We evaluated their performance against the comprehensive geriatric assessment-based frailty index (CGA-FI) and the frailty phenotype (FP) in Round 11 and Round 9.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 1,527 FFS and 1,457 MA beneficiaries in Round 11, frailty prevalence was 34.2% and 35.5%, respectively, by CGA-FI ≥0.25, and 13.3% and 16.2%, respectively, by FP. Across FFS and MA populations, the CFI, which prioritizes specificity and positive predictive value, classified 10-12% of the overall population and 30-36% of those with prior hospitalization as frail, whereas the VA-FI and HFRS, which emphasize sensitivity, classified 53-71% of the overall population and 56-87% of those with prior hospitalization as frail. Although claims-based frailty measures performed similarly across FFS and MA populations, their discriminatory ability was higher for CGA-FI ≥0.25 (C-statistics: CFI, 0.79-0.82; VA-FI, 0.77-0.82; HFRS, 0.63-0.77) than for FP (CFI, 0.71-0.77; VA-FI, 0.67-0.75; HFRS, 0.60-0.74). Performance was consistent by race and survey rounds, with modestly better discrimination in women than men.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Claims-based frailty measures are scalable tools for contemporary FFS and MA populations. However applying published thresholds led to differences in frailty prevalence and model performances. Thresholds should therefore be tailored to the intended.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Performance of Claims-based Frailty Indices in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sleep duration has well-established U-shaped associations with cognitive health, but research has largely ignored spousal interdependence. This study examined actor and partner effects of sleep duration on global cognition in middle-aged and older Chinese couples, testing whether associations differed by sex.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from CHARLS waves 1-4 (2011-2018). The analytical sample comprised 4,260 couples (8,520 individuals) aged ≥45 years living a married, two-person, mixed-sex household. Global cognition was assessed with a composite battery adapted from the Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status and Chinese Mini-Mental State Examination; nocturnal sleep and napping durations were self-reported. Actor-Partner Interdependence Models with quadratic terms examined actor effects (own sleep predicting own cognition) and partner effects (own sleep predicting spouse’s cognition), with false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted q-values and sex-equality tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Significant inverted U-shaped actor effects were found for wives (β=-0.010, 95% CI: -0.014, -0.005, p &lt; 0.001) and husbands (β=-0.011, 95% CI: -0.016, -0.006, p &lt; 0.001); both survived FDR correction (q = 0.002, q &lt; 0.001). Husbands’ sleep was nominally associated with wives’ cognition similarly (β=-0.005, p = 0.025), while wives’ sleep was not associated with husbands’ cognition (p = 0.618). The husband-to-wife association did not survive FDR correction (q = 0.239), and sex-equality tests were non-significant (χ²(9)=9.35, p = 0.406). Napping showed limited, largely non-significant associations with cognition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Own nocturnal sleep duration shows a robust, symmetric inverted U-shaped association with cognitive function in both spouses. The possible husband-to-wife partner effect did not survive correction for multiple testing and warrants adequately powered investigation before informing couple-based clinical recommendations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Wife-Husband Differences in the Associations Between Sleep Durations and Global Cognition Among Middle-Aged and Older Married Couples in China: A Longitudinal Dyadic Analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our study examined how social disconnection, neighborhood contexts, and cognitive function trajectories are jointly and interactively associated among middle-aged and older Black adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data came from non-Hispanic Black participants aged 51 and older (n = 1,791) from the Health and Retirement Study. Cognitive health was measured by a global cognitive function summary score. Social disconnectedness was measured by three types of social isolation (from extended family, adult children, and friends) and loneliness (UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale). Neighborhood contextual factors included neighborhood social cohesion and physical disadvantage. Covariables included age, sex, education, marital status, and living arrangements. We used group-based trajectory modeling to test the study objectives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified four global cognitive function trajectories: low and declining (14% of sample), moderate and declining (29%), moderate and stable (40%), and high and stable (17%). Multivariable models indicated that neighborhood physical disadvantage (RRR=.61, 95%CI[0.40, 0.92]) and social cohesion (RRR=.42, 95%CI[0.23, .77]) moderated the association between social isolation from extended family and global cognitive function trajectory membership.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our study is among the first to examine cognitive function trajectories with linkages to social disconnectedness and neighborhood contexts among middle-aged and older Black adults. Overall, the results suggest that neighborhood contexts condition how social isolation relates to cognitive trajectories. These findings underscore the importance of considering both social disconnectedness and neighborhood context in explaining heterogeneity in cognitive aging among middle-aged and older Black adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social Isolation, Loneliness, and Cognitive Decline Among Black Americans: The Moderating Role of Neighborhood Context

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>BACKGROUND</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Human aging does not follow a single trajectory. Epigenetic changes offer insight into the heterogeneity in aging by reflecting the combined influence of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors on the timing and progression of age-related changes beyond what chronological age alone can explain. Recent studies in cancer and aging underscore the importance of methylation variability as a marker of biological dysregulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>METHODS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We investigated the role of DNA methylation in aging heterogeneity by performing epigenome-wide differential methylation and variance association analyses in blood samples from 1,445 Canadians aged 45 to 85 from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>RESULTS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified 448 differentially methylated regions and 488 differentially variable regions associated with health decline as measured by the health deficit accumulation Frailty Index, cognitive function, and physical function. These two classes of regions showed minimal overlap, with distinct gene coverage, suggesting that variability contributes a complementary signal to aging heterogeneity. Genes overlapped by differentially methylated regions were enriched for immune and inflammation-related pathways, whereas differentially variable regions highlighted additional localized, CpG‑island–enriched signals shared across health domains, consistent with regionally structured rather than diffuse dysregulation. By integrating significant CpGs from both analyses, we constructed an epigenetic biomarker. The biomarker was associated with all-cause mortality and showed higher discrimination than biomarkers constructed from differential methylation or variability alone, with a similar pattern reproduced in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>CONCLUSIONS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that DNA methylation variability may provide a complementary dimension of epigenetic aging and support further evaluation in larger cohorts with more mortality events.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: DNA methylation variability provides a complementary epigenetic signature of aging heterogeneity: Findings from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging and the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Little is known about long-term risks of hospitalizations among heart failure (HF) older adults at a national level. We identified long-term patterns of hospitalizations following the diagnosis of HF and assessed whether high-risk patients can be identified prior to discharge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is a retrospective cohort study from 2010 to 2020. Fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF during an inpatient stay and followed for up to 5 years. Group-based trajectory models (GBTM) identified 4 trajectories of all-cause hospitalizations during follow-up. LASSO regression was used to identify patients’ baseline characteristics to predict their hospitalization trajectories. Model discrimination was assessed using C-statistics and calibration was evaluated using expected-to-observed ratios.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 84,597 Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF (mean age: 77.4 [± 7.1] years and 58.3% male), we identified 4 distinct trajectories of hospitalizations: Group 1 (n = 19,340; 22.9%) had consistently “low risks” of hospitalization, Group 2 (n = 53,922; 57.9%) had elevated risks shortly after discharge (“high-to-low risk”), Group 3 (n = 5,035; 9.8%) had elevated risks at later stages of illness (“low-to-high risk”), and Group 4 (n = 6,300; 9.4%) had consistently “high risks” of hospitalization. Models were well-calibrated predicting hospitalization trajectories (compared to low-risk patients [Group 1]), and C-statistics were 0.65 (Group 2), 0.68 (Group 3), and 0.79 (Group 4). Discrimination was consistently better among patients ≤70 years and calibration remained excellent across all subgroups with expected-to-observed ratios near 1.0.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-risk HF patients could be identified at the time-of-diagnosis using routinely available clinical characteristics, enabling targeted interventions during critical periods to improve long-term outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Longitudinal Trajectories of Hospitalizations in U.S. Older Adults with Heart Failure

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aging is accompanied by changes in body composition and cognition. Although adiposity has been linked to metabolic dysfunction and dementia risk, associations with specific cognitive domains in later life remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study examined associations between adiposity and cognitive performance in 769 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (70–94 years) from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA). Adiposity was assessed using anthropometric measures (body mass index, waist circumference) and MRI-derived regional fat volumes, including visceral and abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue. Cognitive performance was evaluated using a screening measure (Montreal Cognitive Assessment), processing speed (Digit Symbol Coding Test), executive function (Trail Making Test B), and memory (California Verbal Learning Test–II Short Form). Multivariable linear regression models were sequentially adjusted for demographic, cardiometabolic, psychosocial, and behavioral factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Greater age was associated with lower adiposity and poorer cognitive performance (p &lt; 0.05). Most adiposity measures were inversely associated with processing speed after adjustment for age, sex, race, and testing site (p &lt; 0.05). These associations generally persisted after adjustment for cardiometabolic conditions and were attenuated after inclusion of education, depressive symptoms, and behavioral covariates. No significant associations were observed between adiposity and executive function. Memory outcomes showed modest, exploratory associations with abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue measures only in fully adjusted models (p = 0.03–0.07).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In healthy older adults, adiposity is most consistently related to processing speed, whereas associations with memory and executive function are weaker or absent. Processing speed may be especially sensitive to adiposity-related differences. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Adiposity and Cognitive Performance in Older Men and Women from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA)

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aging is the strongest risk factor for most chronic diseases, yet aging-related diseases (ARDs) lack consistent, data-driven definitions. Prior work has proposed frameworks to classify ARDs based on age-specific onset patterns, but applications have largely relied on demographically homogeneous populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We extended a data-driven framework integrating unsupervised clustering and actuarial modeling to electronic health record data from 633,547 participants in the U.S. All of Us Research Program. Age-specific onset rates for 274 high-burden diseases between ages 21 and 74 were analyzed. Standardized onset curves were grouped using hierarchical agglomerative clustering. Aging-related patterns were assessed with Gompertz and Gompertz-Makeham (GM) models to quantify age-dependent increases in disease onset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eleven clusters of disease onset trajectories were identified, with four main clusters encompassing 96.0% of diseases. Two clusters exhibited pronounced late-life increases in onset rate, while one showed earlier but moderate age-related increases, and another displayed largely age-independent patterns. Cardiovascular diseases and cancers were enriched in clusters with strong aging-related onset trajectories. Overall, 165 diseases demonstrated strong evidence of being aging-related, characterized by positive Gompertz age coefficients and good GM model fit. Median onset ages varied across clusters and disease categories and showed statistically significant discrepancies compared with U.K. populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a large, racially diverse U.S. cohort, we identified distinct ARD clusters with shared age-related onset patterns. These findings extend prior work to a more diverse population and support integrated clustering and actuarial approaches to systematically define ARDs and inform aging research and public health strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Aging-Related Diseases in the U.S. Population: A Data-Driven Approach Using All of Us Electronic Health Record Data

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>People who care for a family member with dementia alongside paid work often experience role conflict. This study explores whether work-care role conflict (WCRC) modifies the effectiveness of Draw Care, an online and culturally-adapted carer support intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Secondary exploratory analysis of a single-blind, parallel-group trial (August 2023–November 2024) that compared Draw Care against waitlist control in adult carers from diverse linguistic backgrounds. To formally test whether WCRC moderated the effect of the Draw-Care intervention, we ran a full-sample linear mixed model that included a three-way interaction between time-point, treatment group and an indicator of WCRC. WCRC was operationalised as self-report of missed work or reduced productivity due to competing care and employment demands. Outcomes included carer burden, mood, quality of life, and productivity/ activity impairment at 6 and 12 weeks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-two of 93 carers reported WCRC. Reductions in caregiver burden due to treatment at 6 weeks (-10.00; 95% CI -19.70 to -0.31, p = 0.043) and 12 weeks (-9.56; 95% CI -18.83 to -0.29, p = 0.043) were significantly larger in participants with WCRC than without. This moderating effect of WCRC was driven by a robust, absolute reduction in caregiver burden in intervention group participants with WCRC over the initial 6 weeks (-7.19, 95%CI: -12.72 to -1.67, p = 0.011), with much of this improvement preserved at 12 weeks (-6.85, 95%CI: -12.17 to -1.53, p = 0.012).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>WCRC appears to modify the effectiveness of Draw Care, suggesting that the intervention may be particularly helpful for carers navigating role conflict.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The modifying effect of work-care role conflict on the effectiveness of carer support: Results from the Australian Draw Care randomised clinical trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Heart failure (HF) is a leading cause of hospitalization among older adults and is associated with poor post-discharge outcomes. Multicomponent transitional care programs incorporating telehealth may improve self-management and care transitions; however, their feasibility and preliminary effects require further evaluation in older adults with HF. This study developed and evaluated a solution-focused, telehealth-supported program (SF-TSTCP) integrating structured transitional care, wearable devices, an online platform, and solution-focused approach during telephone follow-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A two-phase design was used. Phase I involved qualitative interviews with older adults with HF to inform intervention development. Phase II was a pilot randomized controlled trial conducted in a tertiary hospital in Southwest China. Fifty-six hospitalized HF patients aged ≥ 60 years were randomized 1:1 to transitional care (TC) or usual care (UC). The SF-TSTCP was delivered from admission through 30 days after discharge. Data were collected at baseline (T0, admission), discharge (T1), 30 days after discharge (T2), and 90 days after discharge (T3). Primary outcomes were feasibility and acceptability (including satisfaction with each program component and willingness to continue); secondary outcomes included discharge preparation, transitional care quality, quality of life, and health service utilization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fifty-two participants (92.9%) completed 90-day follow-up. The SF-TSTCP demonstrated high feasibility, with completion rates of 100% for inpatient components, 92.6% for telephone follow-ups, 85.2% for wearable device use, and 70.4% for weekly platform engagement. Participants reported high satisfaction and willingness to continue the program. Compared with UC, the TC group showed improved discharge preparation, transitional care quality, and quality of life at 30 and 90 days after discharge (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.05 for all comparisons). No significant differences were observed in Unscheduled readmissions, outpatient department visits, or emergency room visits.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The multicomponent SF-TSTCP was feasible, acceptable for older adults with HF. Preliminary findings suggest potential benefits in discharge preparation, transitional care quality, and quality of life. These findings require confirmation in adequately powered trials.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A pilot randomized trial of a solution-focused, telehealth-supported transitional care program in older adults with heart failure

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background/objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging presents challenges for society and healthcare, notably in preventing sarcopenia, a condition that impairs older adults’ quality of life and functionality. This article reviews the current literature on dietary and exercise interventions to evaluate their effectiveness in managing sarcopenia and explore their integration in primary care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic review was conducted under PRISMA guidelines by searching PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Embase, and the Cochrane Library via MeSH terms and the PICOS criteria. The analysis focused on randomized studies involving adults over 65 years of age that assessed nutritional and exercise interventions delivered in primary care settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Six studies, encompassing 444 participants in experimental groups and 226 in control groups, met the inclusion criteria. Combined interventions, physical exercise paired with nutritional supplementation, demonstrated notable improvements in muscle strength, physical function, and body composition. However, the results varied depending on the study design and adherence rates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multidimensional approaches within primary care show promising potential for slowing sarcopenia progression and enhancing quality of life among older adults. Despite encouraging findings, limited research in this area signals the need for further studies emphasizing personalized, sustainable strategies to optimize clinical implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Approach to sarcopenia in older adults: a systematic review of dietary and exercise interventions in the primary care setting

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multimorbidity is prevalent among older adults, but its specific patterns and differential associations with impairments across intrinsic capacity (IC) domains remain under-explored. This study aimed to identify stable multimorbidity patterns in rural older adults using multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) combined with k-means clustering and to examine their independent associations with domain-specific IC impairments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 3,641 community-dwelling older adults with multimorbidity (≥ 2 of 15 chronic conditions) from rural China. MCA was used to reduce dimensionality, followed by k-means clustering to identify multimorbidity patterns. Multivariable logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, education, income, and smoking status, was used to estimate the associations between the identified patterns and impairments in each of the six IC domains (cognition, physical function, vitality, psychology, hearing, and vision), with the high metabolic burden pattern used as the reference.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five stable multimorbidity patterns were identified: high metabolic burden (36.4%), musculoskeletal degenerative (28.4%), gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern (13.8%), cardiovascular-heart failure pattern (13.0%) and respiratory pattern (8.4%). Compared with the high metabolic burden pattern, the gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern was associated with higher odds of vitality impairment (OR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.30–2.21); the cardiovascular-heart failure pattern was associated with higher odds of physical function impairment (OR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.11–1.77); and the gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern, cardiovascular-heart failure pattern, and respiratory pattern were all associated with higher odds of psychological impairment (ORs from 1.61 to 2.27). The respiratory and gastrointestinal-tumor risk patterns were also associated with higher odds of hearing and visual impairments. Notably, the high metabolic burden pattern demonstrated the strongest risk for cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Distinct multimorbidity patterns are differentially associated with specific IC domain impairments. These findings support pattern-oriented risk stratification and targeted functional management in older adults, offering a practical framework for precision geriatric care in resource-limited rural settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Multimorbidity patterns and domain-specific intrinsic capacity impairments among rural older adults: a multiple correspondence analysis and k-means clustering study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malnutrition is common in older adults with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission and is associated with adverse outcomes. We aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI) and its early change (ΔPNI) for predicting ICU mortality and to compare their performance with the modified Nutrition Risk in the Critically Ill (mNUTRIC) score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This single-center retrospective study included 319 older adults (aged ≥ 65 years) with AECOPD admitted to the ICU. PNI was calculated at admission and on day 3, and ΔPNI was defined as the difference between these values. The mNUTRIC score was calculated at admission. The primary outcome was ICU mortality. Discriminative performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression, and survival was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      ICU mortality was 19.8%. The mNUTRIC score demonstrated strong discriminative ability for predicting ICU mortality (AUC 0.852), significantly higher than that of PNI (AUC 0.664;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.0001). In multivariable analysis, the mNUTRIC score remained an independent predictor of ICU mortality (OR 2.50;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Although hypertension was associated with lower mortality in univariate analysis, this association was not confirmed after adjustment for disease severity. In univariate analysis, ΔPNI did not demonstrate significant prognostic value (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.083), and this was consistent across multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analyses. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly poorer survival among patients with high risk (mNUTRIC ≥ 6) (log-rank
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). In Cox proportional hazards analysis, only mNUTRIC remained independently associated with mortality, whereas neither baseline PNI nor ΔPNI demonstrated an independent association with survival.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In older adults with AECOPD requiring ICU admission, baseline multidimensional risk assessment using the mNUTRIC score was strongly associated with ICU mortality. Among patients who survived and remained in the ICU until day 3, early changes in PNI did not provide meaningful additional prognostic information beyond the baseline assessment. The lack of prognostic significance of ΔPNI was consistent across ROC, multivariable logistic regression, and Cox survival analyses. The apparent inverse association between hypertension and mortality was largely explained by disease severity. Further prospective studies incorporating direct measures of frailty are needed to validate these findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Prognostic value of mNUTRIC and nutritional indices, including early change, for ICU mortality in older adults with AECOPD

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hypertension affects 31.6% of Chinese adults, yet medication nonadherence (30-50%) remains a critical barrier to control. The purpose of this study is to explore the relationship between hypertension knowledge, medication adherence, and lifestyle factors, and their associations with blood pressure control in older hypertensive patients living in the community.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cross-sectional study of 437 hypertensive patients (≥ 65 years) in Taizhou, China (Oct-Dec 2023). Medication adherence was assessed via composite score (0–8, > 6 = good) from four validated questions. Hypertension knowledge was evaluated through structured questionnaires. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Only 35.3% demonstrated good adherence. Intentional non-adherence behaviors (skipping doses, stopping when asymptomatic) and difficulty remembering medications were significantly associated with poor blood pressure control (p < 0.05). Blood pressure control correlated with salt/fat intake regulation and sleep quality (p < 0.001). Polypharmacy, driven by comorbidities, created adherence challenges.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Poor medication adherence, driven primarily by intentional behaviors (e.g., dose skipping, stopping when asymptomatic) and regimen complexity, is strongly associated with poor blood pressure control. Effective interventions must address these specific behavioral and systemic barriers to improve hypertension management in older adults.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthy ageing requires more than total physical activity volume; the context, voluntariness, recovery opportunity, and social meaning of activity may shape how activity relates to health in later life. Guided by the physical activity paradox, this study examined whether leisure-time exercise moderates the longitudinal association between agricultural labor and self-rated health among older Chinese adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from five waves of the China Family Panel Studies (2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, and 2018). The analytical sample included 18,050 person-wave observations from 9,449 adults aged 60 years and older. Self-rated health was modeled as a five-point outcome in individual fixed-effects linear models. Standard errors were clustered at the individual level. Agricultural labor, leisure-time exercise, and their interaction were the principal explanatory variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the fully adjusted interaction model, agricultural labor was associated with lower self-rated health among respondents who did not exercise (β = −0.753, 95% CI − 0.856 to − 0.651,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Leisure-time exercise showed a small but statistically non-significant association with self-rated health among respondents not engaged in agricultural labor (β = 0.047, 95% CI − 0.006 to 0.099,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.082). The agricultural labor × leisure-time exercise interaction was positive (β = 0.898, 95% CI 0.793 to 1.002,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), consistent with a less negative agricultural labor-SRH pattern among respondents who exercised. Age-stratified interaction estimates were numerically larger among adults aged ≥ 70 years than among those aged 60–69 years; however, formal between-group differences were not tested.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Agricultural labor and leisure-time exercise were not interchangeable activity domains in this longitudinal sample. Agricultural labor was related to lower self-rated health, the general main association of exercise was not statistically significant in the fully adjusted interaction model, and the interaction suggested that the exercise-health association was contingent on agricultural labor status. Rural healthy-ageing strategies should distinguish physically demanding work from voluntary, recovery-sensitive exercise while avoiding causal claims from observational associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The physical activity paradox in later life: does leisure-time exercise modify the association between agricultural labor and self-rated health?

                    <jats:p>Anthropometric thresholds used to define obesity and central obesity are largely derived from younger populations, although aging is accompanied by marked alterations in body composition and fat distribution.                   </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional analysis of the NutriCare study, 387 relatively independent residents aged 65–101 years from 20 nursing homes were assessed. Standardized anthropometry was performed, and body composition was estimated using bioimpedance spectroscopy. Obesity was defined using WHO BMI criteria, and central obesity using established WC cut-offs for Caucasian populations. Associations with fasting glucose and documented type 2 diabetes (T2D) were examined separately in men and women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants (220 women, 167 men; mean age 81 ± 8 years) had a high burden of excess adiposity, with central obesity more frequent than BMI-defined obesity. Advancing age was accompanied by reductions in BMI in both sexes, with declining fat mass in men and decreasing WC in women. The correlation between BMI and WC attenuated with increasing age. Both adiposity indicators were associated with higher fasting glucose concentrations, while a higher prevalence of documented T2D was observed only among participants with BMI-defined obesity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In very old adults, central obesity is common, yet the relationship between BMI, WC, and metabolic risk may differ from patterns observed in younger populations. These exploratory findings suggest that the diminishing agreement between BMI and WC at higher age may indicate that conventional anthropometric thresholds do not fully capture adiposity-related risk in late life. Further research in larger and more diverse cohorts is needed to inform age- and sex-specific approaches to obesity assessment in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study was registered in clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05389618) on 25.05.2022.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Polypharmacy and multimorbidity make medication review in older adults a high-stakes clinical task. Large language models (LLMs) may support medication review, but whether item-level concordance with explicit prescribing criteria reflects expert-rated reasoning quality and safety prioritisation is uncertain. We compared the quality and safety of outputs generated by three LLMs using a two-stage evaluation framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this two-stage comparative vignette-based benchmark evaluation, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Pro responded to 20 standardised geriatric pharmacotherapy vignettes representing fictional older adults aged 72–88 years across four clinical domains. Each vignette contained three potentially inappropriate medications and one clinically relevant START-type omission anchored to the AGS Beers Criteria and STOPP/START version 3. Models received an identical master prompt under default end-user settings; memory features were disabled where available and separate sessions were used for each vignette. Two geriatricians, blinded to model identity, independently rated anonymised outputs using a 100-point rubric comprising medication review output quality (0–80) and critical safety-risk prioritisation (0–20). Stage 1 assessed answer-key concordance; exploratory Stage 2 characterised clinically contextualised error patterns. Comparisons used Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Cochran’s Q, and exact McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Stage 1 concordance was uniformly high, with limited between-model discrimination. Expert-rated total scores differed across models (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.700): Gemini 3 Pro scored highest (97.93 ± 2.33; 95% CI 96.83–99.02), followed by Claude Sonnet 4.5 (93.90 ± 3.37) and GPT-5.2 (89.85 ± 5.23); all pairwise comparisons were significant, with large standardised effect sizes (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.55–0.61). Safety scores showed the same ranking (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.861;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.52–0.62). Reliability of averaged total ratings was high (ICC(A,2) = 0.935; 95% CI 0.897–0.957). In the exploratory Stage 2 error analysis, Gemini was less frequently flagged than GPT-5.2 for superficial reasoning, weak emphasis on life-threatening risk, and any flagged error, and less frequently than Claude Sonnet 4.5 for weak emphasis on life-threatening risk and any flagged error.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within this vignette-based benchmark, high item-level concordance did not ensure high expert-rated output quality or safety prioritisation. Models also differed in safety prioritisation and in the pattern of flagged errors. These findings support supervised use of LLMs and evaluation approaches that assess reasoning and prioritisation as well as target detection. They should not be interpreted as evidence that one model is clinically superior in real-world practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical trial not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
