                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging is one of the most important demographic transitions of the twenty-first century and is creating new demands for health and social welfare systems. In Iran, rapid population aging, expanding digital transformation, and persistent inequities in access to care have made the future of Digital Health Services (DHS) for older adults increasingly uncertain. This study aimed to explore plausible future pathways for the development of DHS for older adults in Iran using the scenario planning approach by Global Business Network (GBN) method.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This exploratory qualitative futures study was conducted in three phases using the GBN scenario planning method. In the first phase, five Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) were held to identify factors influencing the future of DHS for older adults in Iran. These factors were organized according to the STEEP (Social, Technological, Economic, Environmental, and Political) framework into social, technological, environmental, economic, and political dimensions. In the second phase, an expert panel scored the identified factors according to importance and uncertainty. In the third phase, a scenario-building workshop was conducted to develop future scenarios based on the key scenario-driving axes, where the intersecting axes formed the basis of a two-dimensional scenario framework generating four distinct future scenarios for the 2035 horizon.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 70 variables influencing the future of older adult care were initially identified, of which 20 key variables remained after consolidation and expert evaluation. The findings identified Governance and Political–Economic (G-PE) support, together with the Technological Advancement and Innovations (TAI), as the two principal drivers shaping future scenarios of older adult care in Iran. Based on these drivers, four plausible scenarios were developed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The future of older adult care in Iran will depend not only on TAI but also on the strength of G-PE integration. The scenarios showed that technology can either improve care quality and accessibility or intensify inequality and system fragmentation, depending on institutional capacity and regulatory effectiveness. The study highlights the need for a national integrated roadmap to align governance, digital platforms, and health and social care policies toward resilient, equitable, and human-centered older adult care systems.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Peripheral artery disease is a common vascular condition associated with impaired physical function and reduced quality of life in older adults. Although step volume and stepping intensity have been linked to cardiovascular health, the associations of intensity-specific step counts, cadence, and short-bout step accumulation with peripheral artery disease remain unclear. The concept of “exercise snacks,” characterized by brief, intermittent bouts of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, provides a useful framework for examining such activity patterns in free-living settings. This study examined the associations of objectively measured step counts, cadence, and bout-specific step accumulation with peripheral artery disease among community-dwelling older women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 1053 community-dwelling women aged 60–70 years from the Physical Activity and Health in Older Women Study. Step-based metrics were assessed using a waist-worn ActiGraph accelerometer over seven consecutive days. Steps were categorized as light-intensity physical activity or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. Step cadence and bout-specific step accumulation (≥ 3, ≥ 5, and ≥ 10 min) were also derived. Peripheral artery disease was defined as an ankle–brachial index ≤ 0.90. Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to evaluate associations between step-based metrics and peripheral artery disease. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using the lower ankle–brachial index value from either leg as a continuous outcome and supplementary parsimonious regression models to reduce the potential influence of model overfitting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      After full adjustment, more steps accumulated during moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (odds ratio = 0.696, 95% confidence interval: 0.531–0.912,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.009) and higher cadence during moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (odds ratio = 0.967, 95% confidence interval: 0.952–0.983,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) were associated with lower odds of peripheral artery disease, whereas steps and cadence during light-intensity physical activity showed no significant associations. Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity steps accumulated in ≥ 3- and ≥ 5-minute bouts were significantly associated with lower odds of peripheral artery disease, whereas findings for ≥ 10-minute bouts were less robust in sensitivity analyses using ankle–brachial index as a continuous outcome. Restricted cubic spline analyses showed a non-linear inverse association between moderate-to-vigorous physical activity steps and peripheral artery disease, with an exploratory slope change at approximately 2,134 steps per day, and a linear inverse association for moderate-to-vigorous physical activity cadence using 71 steps per minute as the reference.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher moderate-to-vigorous physical activity–related step counts, faster cadence, and greater accumulation of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity in short bouts were associated with lower odds of peripheral artery disease among older women, whereas light-intensity physical activity–related metrics were not. These findings highlight intensity-related and short-bout walking patterns that warrant further investigation but do not support specific behavioral recommendations because of the cross-sectional study design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations of exercise snack–related step metrics with peripheral artery disease in older women: a cross-sectional study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Loneliness is a prevalent public health and care concern among community-dwelling older adults. While cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and social support theory provide useful frameworks for addressing emotional and social loneliness, there remains a gap in translating these theories into structured, culturally tailored interventions within primary care settings. Guided by the Medical Research Council (MRC) framework, this study describes the development of a theory-driven hybrid intervention to reduce loneliness among community-dwelling older adults in China.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intervention development was informed by a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify effective loneliness interventions. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with community-dwelling older adults to explore intervention needs, preferred content, and delivery logistics. An initial draft was refined through formative pilot testing, with feedback informing the modification and finalization of the hybrid intervention for delivery in community healthcare settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evidence synthesis identified the most effective interventions in terms of content, delivery modes, and contact approaches. In the qualitative findings, participants expressed interest in psychological support alongside physical activities, health education, smartphone skills, and fraud prevention. Perceived participation barriers included time constraints, perceived lack of need or interest, transportation, health concerns, and mistrust and difficulty understanding program content. Perceived facilitators included perceived usefulness, positive group atmosphere, and supportive facilitation and enabling conditions. Pilot feedback led to cultural tailoring, incorporation of locally relevant examples and traditional exercises, and pacing adjustments. The finalized intervention comprised six group sessions integrating psychosocial and practical components, supplemented by home practice and digital support via WeChat.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides a transparent account of utilizing the MRC framework to develop a culturally tailored, theory-based hybrid intervention for loneliness among older adults. This systematic process integrated evidence synthesis, stakeholder perspectives, and formative pilot feedback to refine the intervention, providing a foundation for subsequent evaluation of its feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness in community healthcare settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to electronic health record (EHR) data in hospital settings, its use in long-term care (LTC) facilities remains unexplored. Limited information technology infrastructure and unique challenges in LTC settings require a comprehensive examination of AI’s potential to enhance care quality and operational efficiency. This scoping review aimed to identify and map current AI applications utilizing EHR data in LTC facilities to inform future research and practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews was used as a guideline to structure the review topics. The protocol of this scoping review was registered on the Open Science Framework. The inclusion criteria were EHR (participants), AI (concept), and LTC facilities (context), with no date restrictions, but limited to original articles published in English. A systematic search was performed on MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library databases, and SCOPUS by information specialists.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The search included original articles published in English up to October 10, 2024. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Most were retrospective studies (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 7), alongside two longitudinal and one development study. AI methods included natural language processing, machine learning algorithms (e.g., XGBoost, Random Forest), Bayesian networks, and rule-based reasoning. Applications focused on predicting outcomes such as dementia-related symptoms, malnutrition, pressure injuries, delirium, falls, frailty, urinary tract infections, mortality, and nurse staffing optimization. Data sources included large-scale EHR datasets from nursing homes, assisted living facilities, and senior care communities, often containing over 1,000 resident records or 30,000 clinical notes.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI applications in LTC settings show promise for enhancing predictive accuracy and care quality. However, current evidence is limited, and further research is needed to improve model generalizability, validate results prospectively, and integrate AI into routine practice in diverse aged care environments.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community exergaming may help older adults remain physically active by combining movement, enjoyment, and social interaction, but less is known about whether observed changes persist after supervised delivery ends in real-world community settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated immediate and maintenance-related outcomes of the International Singapore Intergenerational National Games, a community-delivered exergaming program for older adults in Singapore. We examined positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, habit strength, physical activity, and exploratory implementation determinants aligned with the capability, opportunity, and motivation–behavior (COM-B) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a multi-wave observational evaluation from October 2025 to January 2026 among 280 older adults recruited from 14 senior activity centers or active aging centers in Singapore. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately after an 8-week supervised training phase (T1), after a 4-week unsupervised free-play phase (T2), and at a later follow-up for selected measures in 6 centers (T3). Immediate within-person changes were examined using 2-tailed paired
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      tests. Maintenance-related trajectories were examined using adjusted linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined whether COM-B–aligned capability, opportunity, and motivation composites were associated with physical activity trajectories.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants had a mean age of 72.54 (SD 6.15) years, and 77.1% (216/280) were female. From T0 to T1, mean positive mental health increased from 55.19 (SD 9.79) to 57.59 (SD 8.70; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.28;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), mean intrinsic motivation increased from 5.94 (SD 1.00) to 6.29 (SD 0.81; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.40;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), and mean habit strength increased from 3.34 (SD 1.11) to 3.81 (SD 0.84; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.42;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). In adjusted mixed models, habit strength remained higher at T2 than at baseline (β=0.362, 95% CI .113-.611;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.005), and intrinsic motivation remained higher at T2 (β=0.397, 95% CI .156-.638;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.001) and T3 (β=0.305, 95% CI .009-.601;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04). Positive mental health was higher immediately after supervised training (β=4.140, 95% CI 2.169-6.111;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) and at T2 (β=7.390, 95% CI 5.370-9.410;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) than at baseline. Among the COM-B domains, only opportunity was associated with greater immediate posttraining physical activity improvement (time × opportunity interaction β=26.464, 95% CI 3.191-49.737;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), with no evidence of a sustained interaction at T2.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this observational evaluation, positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, and habit strength were higher at T2 than at baseline among respondents with available follow-up data, and intrinsic motivation was also higher at the selected-center T3 follow-up. Because this study lacked a control group and attrition increased over time, these findings represent observed longitudinal trajectories rather than causal evidence of program effectiveness. Opportunity-related supports such as access, reminders, routines, staff facilitation, and peer participation may be useful when community exergaming transitions from supervised delivery to reduced-intensity free play, although this interpretation remains exploratory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Community Exergaming and Maintenance-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: Multi-Wave Observational Evaluation

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Resident-to-resident aggression (RRA) is the most common form of elder mistreatment in long-term care settings. Although race/ethnicity is likely a contributing factor, research has been limited in examining the role of residents’ race and ethnicity in RRA. We sought to define and qualitatively examine the predisposing factors and acute precipitants of race/ethnicity-related resident-to-resident aggression (RE-RRA).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by the socioecological model, events-based perspective, and conceptual work on stigma-based aggression, we developed qualitative interview and data analytical guides. We conducted nine focus groups and twelve in-depth interviews with 81 nursing home staff from multiple clinical and non-clinical roles across two long-term care facilities on the U.S. East Coast. We coded qualitative data using a deductive thematic qualitative approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RE-RRA appeared to be a recurring interpersonal dynamic, though its full scope is likely under-detected and under-recognized. We identified five major types of RE-RRA, including physical violence, microaggression, social exclusion, and avoidance. Ten predisposing factors and eight acute precipitants uniquely contributed to RE-RRA, highlighting the importance of considering distinct race- and ethnicity-related elements in prevention research. We summarized our findings in a conceptual framework for RE-RRA that may be useful for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RE-RRA is a distinct phenomenon shaped by identifiable predisposing and precipitating factors, offering opportunities for future prevention and intervention development. These findings underscore the importance of integrating RE-RRA within staff education, existing clinical governance structures, including incident reporting, and quality improvement processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Palliative care (PC) consultation outcomes in nursing homes (NHs) are often assessed using health systems' clinical and utilization metrics rather than outcomes from the perspective of the key partners who provide and sustain it. This study was designed to identify meaningful PC consultation outcomes from the perspectives of NH staff, PC consultants, and NH/PC agency directors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the team conducted semi-structured interviews with key partners from 14 NHs in the Eastern United States. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using conventional content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants (N = 33) included NH staff (e.g., primary care providers and nurses), PC consultants (e.g., PC physicians and PC nurse practitioners), and leaders (e.g., NH directors and PC agency directors). Key partners reported meaningful outcomes in four domains: resident, family, NH staff, and NH facility. Resident outcomes included goal-concordant care, symptom management, hospitalization rates, and understanding of care choices and control. Family outcomes included shared decision-making, understanding of the resident’s disease trajectory and management measures, and feeling supported. NH staff outcomes included capacity to provide high-quality care and emotional support. Lastly, NH facility outcomes included filling care gaps, facility reputation, and organizational morale.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight multi-domain and interdependent PC consultation outcomes across residents, families, staff, and NH facilities that may be overlooked in existing evaluation frameworks. <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ageism is defined as stereotypes, prejudices, and discrimination toward people because of their age. It represents a substantial public health concern given its high prevalence and extensive impact on the health and well-being of older persons. Although interventions to reduce ageism toward older persons among younger persons as agents of ageism exist, much less is known about interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism toward older persons among older persons. This theoretical paper addresses the gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for the development of interventions to reduce ageism among older persons in the second half of life. Drawing on established theories, such as contact theory, terror management theory, stereotype embodiment theory, and social identity theory, we propose various mechanisms through which ageism among older persons can be reduced. The paper explores theoretical assumptions about which interventions work for whom and why to guide further empirical research on the reduction of ageism in the second half of life. We argue that although at the present time, effective interventions to reduce ageism among older persons are scarce, there are many theoretical avenues that may prove effective.</jats:p>
title: There must be fifty ways to reduce ageism: A theoretical perspective on possible interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism among older persons

                  <jats:p>This manuscript analyzes the literary, social and cultural representations of dementia in Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019).                     <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ageism in healthcare contributes to undertreatment, dismissive communication, and age-based exclusions from care, yet no psychometrically validated, patient-reported measure captures older adults’ perceptions of age-based bias during clinical encounters.                   <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Items adapted from four validated discrimination measures plus two new items were administered to community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older in three independent, predominantly non-Hispanic White samples (Ns = 223, 349, 361) recruited through Prolific within the United States.                     <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Study 1 identified two correlated factors, Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism, corroborated by parallel analysis and Velicer’s MAP test. Study 2 indicated that a 20-item model fit poorly and that removing three items produced a refined 17-item model.                     <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 17-item ATHP is a psychometrically sound, healthcare-specific measure distinguishing interpersonal from institutional ageism, equipping researchers, health systems, and policymakers to monitor age-based bias and evaluate interventions.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As the prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults is rising, challenges regarding their end-of-life healthcare choices are increasingly relevant. To address knowledge gaps regarding decision-making, we explored how older adults with multimorbidity, their relatives and involved healthcare professionals experienced end-of-life healthcare choices, how their experiences related to each other and how these choices occurred in interactions between them over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a multiperspective, longitudinal, interview and observation study with a phenomenological and ethnographic approach. We followed nine six-month patient trajectories with eleven relatives and 58 healthcare professionals and conducted 73 observations of patient-healthcare professional interactions and 63 interviews.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The meaning of end-of-life healthcare choices of older people with multimorbidity was essentially understood as an ongoing, entangled, existential and relational process, shaped by, yet also transcending, healthcare contexts. This process was characterized by four tensions: (i) the experience of not having a choice, but making decisions nonetheless; (ii) the existential experience and the medical gaze; (iii) the importance of relatives and their limited role in healthcare; and (iv) navigating fragmented healthcare with interrelated conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthcare professionals’ limited insight into patients’ and relatives’ personal, existential perspectives and relational contexts calls for a better exploration of their lifeworld to ensure the best possible alignment of healthcare decisions with patients’ and relatives’ needs and values. Older adults with multimorbidity are inadequately supported by fragmented healthcare systems, and efforts to improve this should consider existential, relational and systemic factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: “I don’t know whether I really have choices”: a multiperspective and longitudinal exploration of healthcare choices of older adults with multimorbidity

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the influence of respondents’ and informants’ gender on informants’ assessments of cognitive functioning in population studies in the United States and Mexico.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines differences in the composition and size of the close social network among older adults in same-sex and different-sex coresidential unions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using pooled, probability-based, cross-sectional data from the 2006–2022 Health and Retirement Study, weighted fractional probit and negative binomial regression models were estimated to examine differences in close network composition (proportions of close children, immediate family members, and friends) and network size (number of close ties).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with older adults in different-sex unions, those in same-sex unions reported a higher proportion of friends and a lower proportion of children and immediate family members in their close network, though overall network size was comparable. Supplemental analyses suggested heterogeneity in these patterns. The same-sex versus different-sex gap in friend composition was larger among males than females and was similarly larger among those who were cohabiting than married. Finally, in terms of network size, males in same-sex couples reported smaller close networks than males in different-sex couples, whereas network size was equivalent between females in same-sex and different-sex couples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Beyond their partners, older adults in same-sex unions cultivate distinctly friend-centered close networks. This pattern reflects a history of intentionally built chosen ties that queers dominant assumptions about who partnered older adults designate as close. These findings affirm the importance of policies and practices that acknowledge diverse family arrangements, particularly those rooted in chosen kinship, as a fundamental step toward achieving social equity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Composition and size of close social networks among older adults in same-sex and different-sex couples

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intergenerational engagement—here referring to time spent with younger family members—can promote health and happiness. Across adulthood, and particularly in later life, intergenerational engagement represents a potentially meaningful form of social involvement. Using intensive longitudinal methods, we investigated how intergenerational engagement is associated with daily emotional experience and physical activity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, 265 participants aged 23–92 completed a 9-day daily diary protocol assessing their intergenerational engagement and emotional experiences; objective physical activity during this period was assessed via tracking steps taken and sedentary minutes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multilevel models revealed significant within-person associations between intergenerational engagement and both emotional experience and physical activity. On days older adult participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater high-arousal positive emotion (happiness, enthusiasm, excitement) during the day. Across the age span of the sample, on days participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater low-arousal positive emotion (contentment, relaxation, calm) before bed. Finally, both objective metrics revealed greater physical activity on days with greater intergenerational engagement, whereas other social engagement was unassociated with steps taken or sedentary minutes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight intergenerational engagement as a meaningful daily-life context for both positive emotional experiences and physical activity. For older adults in particular, intergenerational engagement may represent a naturally occurring pathway through which emotionally meaningful social ties support both emotional well-being and opportunities for everyday movement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: More positive and more active: Effects of daily intergenerational engagement on emotion and physical activity

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigated how grandchild care intensity and community environment influenced frailty trajectories among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, examining whether effects vary by initial frailty status and are moderated by community environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2013, 2015, 2018) combined with 2011 community data, this study included 13,531 respondents (40,593 observations) across 442 communities. Marginal structural models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were employed to mitigate selection bias. Weighted regressions with community-clustered robust standard errors were constructed, with subgroup analyses stratified by baseline frailty status (non-frail, pre-frail, frail).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While grandchild care showed a null overall effect in the general population, specific impacts varied significantly by baseline frailty status. Intensive caregiving significantly decelerated frailty progression for non-frail adults, whereas moderate caregiving accelerated longitudinal decline among frail adults. Caregiving showed non-significant impacts on frailty trajectory among pre-frail adults. A supportive community environment exerted protective main effects across all subgroups, with the frail group being most affected. It also magnified the protective effects of intensive caregiving on baseline frailty for the non-frail group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a person–environment fit perspective, this study reveals that the health impacts of grandchild care depend on the fit between individuals’ pre-existing health status and caregiving demands, and the role of community becomes more salient as competence declines. Findings highlight the critical need to prioritize vulnerable frail caregivers in health interventions and underscore community development as a key strategy for facilitating healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Competent to care? Grandchild care and frailty trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults through a person-environment fit lens

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prevalence of bridge jobs, post-career work that bridges between career jobs and workforce exit, has obfuscated the isomorphic link between older adults’ role identities as retirees, named ‘retirement identities’, and their actual labor force status in ways that may well differ by gender. We examine how gender and Social Security eligibility/receipt are associated with retirement identities, and how these identities are associated with the timing of final workforce exit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We track bridge job take-ups and workforce exits of Early Boomers (ages 51-56 in 2004, N = 910) in the Health and Retirement Study 2004-2020. We use multinomial logistic regression to examine predictors of retirement identities by gender, and event history analysis to examine the timing of workforce exit at the intersection of gender, retirement identity, and timing of bridge job take-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings reveal that Social Security receipt is associated with men’s retirement identity formation, but not women’s. For both genders, ordered retirement identities, from ‘not retired’ to ‘completely retired,’ predict the timing of workforce exits. Women in bridge jobs do not always exit the workforce earlier than men when retirement identities are taken into account.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study underscores the changes in retirement as an institutionalized and gendered life course status passage, amplified by the increasing pivoting to bridge jobs, but with considerable variability in self-definitions of retirement status. Our evidence suggests that these identities serve as good signals of older workers’ work attachments and retirement plans, offering helpful insights for policymakers and employers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Bridge jobs and retirement identities: Gendered life course approach to workforce exits among Early Boomers

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior research often reports geographic cognitive health disparities in later life, including across rural-urban contexts. Yet few studies have examined the role of personal social networks in shaping these geographic disparities. This study investigates whether social networks moderate or mediate the association between geographic context and cognitive health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study, which is a state representative sample of adults aged 55 and older. A latent measure of social bridging (i.e., connections to weak and diverse ties) was extracted using personal network data. Cognitive health was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Rurality was defined using the Indiana County Classification. Moderation and mediation pathways were tested using linear regression models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There were no observed rural-urban differences in MoCA scores. Yet the association between social bridging and MoCA was significantly stronger among rural participants compared to urban participants. Rural participants with the lowest levels of social bridging performed significantly worse on the MoCA compared to urban participants with similar bridging levels. These geographic disparities were not present when comparing rural and urban participants with high levels of social bridging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The ability to personally bridge social ties within a network appears to play a more critical role in the cognitive health of rural residents, who live in communities with fewer structural opportunities for social stimulation, compared to urban residents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Personal networks and cognitive health across rural-urban contexts

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Positive social connections are key ingredients for healthy aging. We studied older adults’ shared agreement on loving experiences and individual differences in their decisions-making to unlock critical information about how this developmental group connects socially.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To explore shared agreement on experiences of love, we surveyed a representative sample (N=400) of adults aged 65 years and older in the United States. They evaluated 61 experiences to determine whether older adults believe they typically evoke feelings of love in most people. We used a Bayesian decision tree model to account for individual differences in respondents’ knowledge and decision-making styles when deriving the consensus on these experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found a consensus among older adults on experiences of love. In addition, individual differences in knowledge on love and decision-making styles were meaningfully linked to person-level characteristics: female participants and those with higher levels of compassion had higher levels of knowledge on the consensus, White male participants and those with higher levels of loneliness were more likely to guess the shared agreement when they were uncertain, and non-White participants were more likely to guess “True.”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Experiences of love for older adults include both romantic and non-romantic settings. Older adults tended to have different knowledge levels regarding the consensus on these experiences. Future research could examine whether fostering compassion or raising awareness about these loving experiences in daily life might improve well-being for older adults. Increased knowledge regarding these experiences may decrease misunderstandings or loneliness by sharing more loving experiences with others.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:p>This study examines how exposure to cumulative socioeconomic status (SES) risk in midlife shapes subsequent biological aging among Black American women and tests whether a sense of mastery moderates these associations.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>Using longitudinal data from 334 middle-aged Black American women in the Family and Community Health Study (FACHS), we used hierarchical regression models to test our hypotheses and probed the interaction by estimating conditional differences between high and low mastery across levels of cumulative SES risk.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cumulative SES risk was significantly associated with accelerated aging. After accounting for key environmental, psychosocial, behavioral, and biological confounders, each additional risk factor was associated with an increase in GrimAgeAccel of approximately 0.53 years (6.4 months). Among women with lower mastery, cumulative SES risk was positively and significantly associated with accelerated biological aging, with each additional SES risk factor associated with an increase of approximately 0.59 years (7.1 months) in GrimAge acceleration. Cumulative SES risk was not associated with accelerated aging among women with higher mastery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Consistent with stress process theory, higher mastery was associated with a weaker association between cumulative socioeconomic disadvantage and accelerated aging among middle-aged Black American women. Persistent SES-related disparities in biological aging indicate that upstream sociostructural determinants impose a chronic physiological burden that cannot be addressed by individual coping resources alone. Simultaneously bolstering psychosocial resources and addressing the structural conditions that necessitate such high levels of individual coping may be critical for promoting sustained, population-level improvements in healthy aging.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others’ intentions during fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning (EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant mini-UG decisions estimated individuals’ tendencies to consider intention vs. outcome information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) decisions across age groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings extend prior work on age differences in intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Fairness decision-making in younger and older adults and associated neural indices

We examined the moderating role of race-ethnicity in the association between age and exposure to three weather events. records.abstract: <jats:p>Hurricanes can profoundly affect the delivery of home health (HH) services. records.abstract: <jats:p>Namaste Care is a person-centered intervention for people with dementia in long-term care, particularly those in advanced stages. However, evidence on how staff are trained and supported to deliver Namaste Care remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map training content, delivery formats and support, and training-related outcomes. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, eight databases were searched from inception to May 2026, with additional website and citation searches. Data were synthesized descriptively, and training-related outcomes were mapped against the Kirkpatrick Four-Level Training Evaluation Model. Eleven studies were included. Training commonly addressed core Namaste Care principles and activities, and several programs also included knowledge of dementia and palliative care, as well as communication and relational care skills. Face-to-face workshops and in-service sessions were the most common delivery formats, with some programs also incorporating experiential learning. Follow-up support and practical resources were frequently reported, and family involvement was incorporated into several programs. Staff reactions were generally positive. Learning-related outcomes included greater understanding of the purpose and delivery of Namaste Care and reported improvements in knowledge, attitudes, and self-perceived skills. Some studies reported changes in staff practice, although intended program frequency or duration was not always achieved because of staffing and organizational constraints. Resident, staff, and family caregiver outcomes were mixed and could not be attributed to training alone. Namaste Care training is therefore better understood as part of a broader practice-support strategy rather than as a stand-alone educational activity. However, existing evaluations remain incomplete, with limited evidence linking staff learning to subsequent practice change and wider outcomes.</jats:p>
title: Mapping Namaste Care Training for Staff in Long-Term Care Settings: A Scoping Review

The videos were introduced over an 18-month period in two contrasting care settings in Vancouver, Canada: an acute hospital geriatric unit and a long-term care dementia unit. Nineteen interdisciplinary healthcare providers, including nurses, care aides, and rehabilitation and recreation staff, participated in semi-structured interviews and focus groups after using the videos in routine care. A reflexive thematic analysis was conducted, followed by a later-stage comparison with relevant constructs from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). A participatory research team, including people living with dementia and family caregivers, contributed to study design, interpretation, and theme refinement. Findings showed that time pressures and staffing constraints limited workflow compatibility, particularly because many residents required assistance to operate devices. Limited equipment and unstable internet access further hindered consistent use. Facilitators included motivated staff who acted as catalysts for adoption, the perceived advantages of dementia-friendly videos over general platforms, and staff observations of positive impacts on emotional regulation and participation. Seeing benefits in practice, such as calming distressed patients, reinforced continued use. The study highlights the importance of integrating dementia-friendly videos into existing workflows rather than treating them as additional tasks. Ensuring adequate equipment, supporting motivated staff, and attending to cultural and linguistic relevance are essential for sustainable implementation. These findings offer practical guidance for embedding person-centred digital tools into dementia care.</jats:p>
title: Implementing Dementia-Friendly Videos in Everyday Care: A Qualitative Study of Frontline Staff Experiences

records.abstract: <jats:p>Placement of a relative with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) in residential care is often assumed to reduce caregiver burden. However, little is known about how informal caregivers experience their role after placement. This descriptive phenomenological study explored the lived experiences of 9 informal family caregivers whose relatives with ADRD resided in residential care settings. Semi-structured interviews lasting 60 to 120 minutes were conducted and analyzed using Colaizzi’s method to identify the essential structures of post-placement caregiving. Brief quantitative measures, including the CES-D-10 and the Caregiver Self-Assessment Questionnaire, were collected to contextualize participants’ emotional burden. Six themes emerged: emotional dissonance after placement, cognitive load and decision fatigue, persistence of caregiver identity and responsibility, fragmented systems and resource gaps, crisis-driven transitions, and the need for post-placement support. Participants described caregiving after placement not as an endpoint, but as a reconfigured role marked by ongoing emotional labor, vigilance, advocacy, and decision-making. Although physical caregiving tasks had shifted to staff, caregivers remained deeply involved in monitoring care quality, managing communication, responding to crises, and serving as the primary emotional anchor for their relatives. Quantitative findings reinforced these accounts, with all participants scoring above the CES-D-10 clinical threshold and reporting substantial caregiver distress. Taken together, the findings suggest that caregiving continues in sustained and multidimensional ways after residential placement. Residential care settings should recognize family caregivers as ongoing partners and provide structured orientation, clearer communication pathways, and psychosocial support to address the emotional, cognitive, and relational demands of post-placement caregiving.</jats:p>
title: Continuing the Role: Lived Experiences of Family Caregivers after Placement of a Relative With Dementia in Residential Care

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive reserve (CR) is thought to buffer against the clinical manifestation of dementia, preserving cognitive function despite accumulating pathology. However, less is known about how CR relates to the capacity to independently perform activities of daily living (ADL), particularly among cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults. Here, we investigated this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Baseline data from 1,571 CU participants (mean age: 64.7±7.6; 81.3% female) from the CAN-PROTECT study were analyzed. A composite CR score was derived from education, occupational complexity, and engagement in cognitively stimulating activities. Functional ability was measured using the Standard Assessment of Global Everyday Activities (SAGEA) scale, capturing cognitive, applied cognitive, instrumental, and basic ADL, and mobility. Negative binomial models examined associations between CR and global and domain-specific ADL, adjusting for age, sex, cognition, behaviour, and physical/sensory limitations. Additional models tested the independent contribution of CR components to functional outcomes. Mediation analyses assessed the effect of CR on quality of life (QoL) through ADL abilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher CR was associated with lower global ADL impairment (count ratio=0.58, 95%CI: 0.36-0.94, p = 0.027), driven by 49% less impairment in applied cognitive ADL (95%CI: 0.26-0.97, p = 0.038). Among CR domains, education showed the most consistent association with lower impairment across all ADL domains and was indirectly linked to better QoL through improved function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CR, particularly education, may play an important role in supporting functional abilities and QoL among CU older adults. Enhancing CR may be a promising avenue to promote functional independence and healthy aging, even in the absence of cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cognitive reserve and everyday functioning in cognitively unimpaired older adults: evidence from the CAN-PROTECT study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Brain aging characterized by progressive structural and functional changes, including atrophy of the hippocampus and frontal cortex, reduced neurogenesis and synaptogenesis, and disruptions in network connectivity, collectively impairing memory, attention, and executive functions. However, aging is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous process, with variability in decline and preservation of certain cognitive capacities supported by compensatory mechanisms. Neuroplasticity plays a central role in mitigating age-related losses by enabling functional reorganization and maintaining neural connectivity. This integrative review synthesizes evidence on the effects of physical activity, sensory stimulation, and multisystem interventions on brain aging. Aerobic and multicomponent exercise programs, particularly those lasting 8–24 weeks, have been associated with improvements in hippocampal volume, executive function, and mobility. These benefits appear to be mediated by upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, lactate signaling, and cathepsin B, which support synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and cerebral perfusion. Sensory stimulation enhances neural processing through multisensory integration, strengthening connectivity within attentional and executive networks. Combined interventions that integrate motor, sensory, and cognitive components appear promising and may offer advantages over single‑domain approaches, although direct comparative evidence remains limited. Activities such as dance, proprioceptive training, and musical engagement exemplify sensorimotor integration, promoting cognitive reserve. In addition, emerging technologies, including virtual reality and brain-computer interfaces, further support personalized, neuroplasticity-driven rehabilitation. Together, these findings highlight sensorimotor integration as a central mechanism for preserving cognitive and functional capacity and promoting healthy brain aging.</jats:p>
title: The effects of physical and sensory activities on motor and cognitive functions in the aging brain: a review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>More than one-in-five older adults live in the rural U.S. Adults living in rural U.S. experience significantly higher hypertension prevalence and cardiovascular disease-related mortality compared to their urban counterparts. To extend the literature and provide real-world evidence, the primary objective of this study was to estimate the prevalence of uncontrolled hypertension and to identify factors associated with it among Medicare beneficiaries receiving care in rural South Carolina.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were used from the annual review of Abbeville County Medicare patients diagnosed with hypertension between July 2024 and January 2025. Uncontrolled hypertension was defined as blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg with or without antihypertensive medications. Generalized linear models with a binomial distribution and logit link were used to examine individual, behavioral, clinical, and area-level contextual factors associated with uncontrolled hypertension.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Responses from 813 Medicare beneficiaries with diagnosed hypertension were analyzed: 55.6% females with a mean age (standard deviation) of 73.2±8.48 years. Overall, the prevalence (95% CI) of uncontrolled hypertension was 76.3% (95% CI: 73.2, 79.1). Compared with a healthy weight, being overweight (aOR=2.0; 95% CI: 1.2, 3.3; p =  0.005) or obese (aOR=2.1; 95% CI: 1.1, 2.8; p = 0.010) was associated with higher odds of uncontrolled hypertension. Contrary to previous findings, “most of the time” PA (aOR=1.57; 95% CI: 1.05-2.34; p = 0.027) was associated with a higher likelihood of uncontrolled hypertension compared to no PA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings highlight a high burden of uncontrolled hypertension in a rural Medicare population, underscore the need for objective measures and further studies into the individual, behavioral, clinical, and contextual factors that may contribute to blood pressure control in rural communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: “Uncontrolled Hypertension Among Medicare Beneficiaries in Rural South Carolina.”

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The patterns and determinants of late-life functional decline are not fully understood. We examined disability trajectories in relation to proximity to death among decedents aged 70 years and older, and investigated their associations with sex, age at death, education, cognitive impairment, and chronic conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Harmonised data from six Swedish longitudinal ageing studies (1997–2016) within the National E-infrastructure for Aging Research (NEAR) were used. Participants who died at age 70 years or older and had data on activities of daily living (ADL) from at least two assessments were included (N = 2294, 62% women, mean age at death 89.8 years [SD 6.5]). ADL limitations (0–5 scale) were analysed across four time intervals before death (0–2, &gt;2–4, &gt;4–6, and 6–12 years). Group-based trajectory modelling identified disability trajectories, multinomial logistic regression examined demographic associations, and generalized estimating equations assessed associations of cognitive impairment and chronic conditions with trajectory membership.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three trajectories were identified: constantly low (53%), low-sharply increasing (36%), and high-increasing (11%). Women, those with lower education, and individuals dying at older ages were more likely to follow increasing or persistently high disability trajectories. High-increasing trajectory was associated with higher likelihood of cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For most, ADL limitations remained low until the final two years of life, though distinct trajectories with steady or sharp increases also emerged. Identifying demographic and health-related factors associated with functional decline may inform targeted interventions and help anticipate care needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Disability trajectories in the last years of life: a Swedish longitudinal multi-cohort study

                  <jats:p>Statins have pleiotropic properties beyond LDL cholesterol reduction, including anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects that may influence biological aging and frailty. The primary objective was to compare frailty trajectories in people with HIV using statins for cardiovascular prevention with those not using statins. Secondary objectives included differences in walking speed, short physical performance battery, and hand grip strength. This observational longitudinal study included people with HIV from the Modena HIV Metabolic Clinic (Italy) with no prior statin use at baseline and at least three frailty index (FI) assessments. Baseline was the first visit with a FI assessment; follow-up was the last visit. Statin users and non-users were matched for follow-up duration. Time 0 (T0) was defined as statin initiation. Frailty was assessed with a 34-item FI. To minimize collider bias, lipid variables were excluded from the FI due to their direct relationship with statin exposure. Frailty trajectories and secondary outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed models. Beta-estimates were multiplied by 100 to improve readability. Among 3,444 people with HIV (69% men; median age 44.7 years), 23.1% initiated statins for primary prevention and 2.0% for secondary prevention. Statin users had a more unfavorable cardiometabolic profile at T0. In adjusted models, statin use was associated with a reduction in FI over time (statin*time interaction β=–2.562, 95%-CI –3.176,–1.987). No associations were observed with secondary outcomes. Statins may improve frailty trajectories, mitigate aging-related decline and preserve physical function in people with HIV, supporting a broader role for statins in HIV care.</jats:p>
title: Statin use is associated with improved frailty trajectories in people with HIV
